name: Storboarding
description:
Storyboarding represents an experience as a sequence of illustrated frames. Borrowed from filmmaking, the technique helps designers show how a situation unfolds over time, including context, actions, interactions and transitions.

Storyboards are particularly useful for communicating experiences that extend beyond a single screen or object.
whenToUse: Use storyboarding when the timing and sequence of an experience matter, when communicating a scenario to others, or when exploring how a concept fits into everyday activity.
steps: Define the scenario and central actor.
Identify the beginning and intended outcome.
Break the experience into significant moments.
Sketch each moment as a separate frame.
Show relevant context, people and artefacts.
Add brief annotations or dialogue where needed.
Review the sequence for missing transitions or assumptions.
lookOutFor: A smooth storyboard can conceal friction and uncertainty.
Include moments before and after the direct interaction with the design.
Drawing quality is less important than whether the sequence communicates clearly.

resources.citation: Truong, K. N., Hayes, G. R. & Abowd, G. D. (2006). “Storyboarding: An Empirical Determination of Best Practices and Effective Guidelines.” *DIS 2006*.
